text.en: Raju noticed the new road cut through green fields. "Does progress cost nature?" he asked.

Man and environment are closely linked. People have long depended on their environment and modified it. Farming, industry, transport and urban construction can change landscapes on different scales. This brings both benefit and harm.
Human activities cause deforestation, soil erosion, air and water pollution and climate change. People respond to environmental conditions in different ways. Housing, work and travel can reflect local climate, resources, technology and cultural choices.
Sustainable development aims to meet present needs without making it harder for future generations to meet their own needs. We can save the environment by planting trees, saving water and energy, and reducing waste.

Environment includes the surroundings that affect living things, from climate and soil to buildings and roads. Human settlements link natural and built surroundings.
A new road can improve access to shops, markets and schools. It can also alter drainage or cross a habitat. Study both the intended use and the side effects.

board.text: One change can bring benefits and costs

text.en: Population means the number of people in an area at a stated time. A census is a systematic count used to describe population and related characteristics.
Population can change through births, deaths and migration. People moving in add to the count. People moving out reduce it.

board.text: Population change: births, deaths and migration

text.en: A population count can rise while its growth rate slows. The count describes the total at one time. The rate describes how quickly it changes over an interval.

board.text: Total and rate answer different questions

text.en: Population distribution describes where people live across an area. A map can show clusters around transport routes or flatter land even if the region’s total stays unchanged.
Water supply, work, transport and terrain can influence where settlements grow. No single factor explains every pattern. Compare several clues on the map.

board.text: Settlement patterns can have several causes

text.en: Population density divides population by area. Use a stated unit such as people per square kilometre and compare places measured on the same basis.
District A has six hundred people in three square kilometres. That is two hundred people per square kilometre. For District B, nine hundred over six gives one hundred fifty.
A larger population does not automatically mean greater density. Our District B has more people and more area. Its population is smaller per square kilometre than A’s.
A region’s average density can hide local clusters. One district can have a busy town and wide areas of sparsely populated land within the same boundary.

board.text: An area average does not show every neighbourhood

text.en: A settlement is a place where people live. Settlements can be temporary or permanent. Their size and layout can change when work or travel changes.

board.text: Settlements vary in duration and layout

text.en: Some houses cluster around a shared place such as a well or market. Other houses are scattered across farms, or arranged in a line along a route.
Rural and urban places often depend on one another. Food, workers, services and goods move between them. Their boundaries and official definitions can vary.

board.text: Rural and urban areas exchange goods and services

text.en: Primary activities involve obtaining products or resources from nature. Farming and fishing are examples. Processing raw materials into goods is a secondary activity.

board.text: Primary obtains resources · secondary processes them

text.en: Tertiary activities provide services such as transport, retail or education. Follow a product from a farm to a workshop and then to a store to see the links between activities.
Removing forest can alter habitat, local water movement and soil protection. Whether erosion increases depends partly on rainfall, slope and how the ground is managed.

board.text: Land cover affects several environmental processes

text.en: Air or water pollution can move away from its source. A downstream town may be affected by an upstream activity. Use evidence from more than one place to compare the effect.

board.text: Environmental effects can cross local boundaries

text.en: Burning fossil fuels contributes greenhouse gases that warm the climate. Other environmental changes include waste accumulation and declining habitat quality. Identify which pressure is being discussed.

board.text: Name the environmental problem and its cause

text.en: Sustainable decisions consider livelihoods, resource limits and long-term effects. A project that saves water in one season should also be checked for its future impacts.

board.text: Compare present needs with future resource use

text.en: Imagine a school finding that a large paved area sends water quickly into a drain. Comparing runoff paths can help it consider planted areas and other ways to manage the water.

board.text: Use observations before choosing an improvement

text.en: To assess a proposed action, state what improvement you expect and how to measure it. Useful evidence could include a water meter reading, a waste count or a repeated habitat observation.
Read a human-environment example in two directions. Explain how the surroundings affect people and how the people’s choices may affect those surroundings.

board.text: People and surroundings influence one another

problem.en: District A has 600 people over 3 km² and B has 900 over 6 km². Which district has the higher density?

text.en: Divide each district’s population by its own area.

why.en: The calculations give two hundred for A and one hundred fifty for B.

text.en: Compare the results using the same unit.

why.en: A has the higher density, measured in people per square kilometre.

prompt.en: A friend says Humans do not affect the environment. How will you reply?
